newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: ASEAN says Cambodia ready for July entry.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN says Cambodia ready for July entry.

text.p: Top ASEAN representatives on Monday said Cambodia was fully ready to join the regional group on July 23 despite recent political difficulties.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi, who visited Phnom Penh with Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) Secretary-General Ajit Singh, said he had formally notified Cambodia of its acceptance into the regional club along with Burma and Laos.

"Of course, I also informed them that we have some concerns about the situation in the country. It is our hope that the leaders will be able to resolve whatever problems that they may be having," Badawi told reporters before returning to Kuala Lumpur.
"...It is important that as a member of ASEAN and (if the nation) is stable and peaceful, there are tremendous benefits that they can have...that they never had before," he said.
He added that in separate meetings, co-premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen had told him they understood the importance of political stability.
Spokesmen for Ranariddh and Hun Sen called the meetings a success and said they would do everything necessary to ensure peace in their country and a smooth entry into ASEAN.

ASEAN, which groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam, decided to admit the three new members despite Western pressure to deny Burma membership because of its human rights record and concerns over political instability in Cambodia.
Relations between Ranariddh and Hun Sen have plummeted in the run-up to next year's general elections.

Their increasingly acrimonious relationship has caused considerable tension in the capital and deadlocked the National Assembly, which has been unable to convene to pass key legislation needed for ASEAN membership.
But Foreign Minister Ung Huot told reporters that the legislation was not needed before entry and that nine remaining ASEAN agreements to be signed in Kuala Lumpur in July were only a formality.
More important, he said, was maintaining peace in Cambodia.
"Anything that will affect Cambodia will affect the region, so there is some indirect pressure on Cambodia to get our act together...," he said.
Cambodia was ruled by the notorious Khmer Rouge from 1975 to 1978 during which time more than a million people died from torture, starvation, disease or overwork.
The guerrillas reneged on a 1991 peace pact and are still fighting the coalition government set up after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993.
Badawi and Singh, who are on a tour of the new member countries, returned to Kuala Lumpur on Monday afternoon.
They are scheduled to visit Burma on Tuesday.
